questions.stem: Which of these is a way monoclonal antibodies are used in hospital laboratories?
options: Growing cultures of bacteria faster
Measuring a patient's blood pressure
Killing bacteria on lab equipment
Measuring the levels of hormones in blood, or detecting pathogens
questions.hint: They can stick to one particular chemical in a blood sample.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Monoclonal antibodies are not used to help bacteria grow.
B: Incorrect — Blood pressure is measured with a cuff, not antibodies.
C: Incorrect — Equipment is sterilised with heat or disinfectant, not antibodies.
D: Correct — Because the antibody binds to one target, it can show whether that target is there.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order for making monoclonal antibodies?
options: Combine with tumour cells → stimulate mouse lymphocytes → collect the antibody → clone a single hybridoma
Stimulate mouse lymphocytes → collect and purify the antibody → combine with tumour cells → clone a single hybridoma
Stimulate mouse lymphocytes → combine with tumour cells to make hybridomas → clone a single hybridoma → collect and purify the antibody
Clone a single hybridoma → stimulate mouse lymphocytes → combine with tumour cells → collect the antibody
questions.hint: The cells must make the right antibody before they are fused.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The lymphocytes are stimulated before they are fused, and cloning comes before collection.
B: Incorrect — Large amounts of antibody are only made after the hybridoma is cloned.
C: Correct — The lymphocytes are triggered to make the antibody first, then made able to divide.
D: Incorrect — You can't clone a hybridoma before it has been made.

questions.stem: Why are monoclonal antibodies not yet as widely used as people hoped?
options: They bind to every cell in the body
Only tiny amounts can ever be made
Bacteria quickly become resistant to them
They have caused more side effects than expected
questions.hint: Think about what happened when they were used in patients.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — They are specific to one antigen.
B: Incorrect — Cloned hybridoma cells make large amounts, which can be collected and purified.
C: Incorrect — Resistance is a problem with antibiotics, not the reason here.
D: Correct — This has limited their use in treatment.

questions.stem: A pregnancy test strip contains monoclonal antibodies with a coloured dye attached. They bind to a hormone called HCG, which is only in the urine of pregnant women. Why does a coloured line appear only if the woman is pregnant?
options: The antibodies make HCG when urine touches them
The antibodies destroy HCG, leaving a coloured mark
The antibodies change colour in any urine
The antibodies are specific to HCG, so they only bind and show colour when HCG is present
questions.hint: Ask yourself what the antibodies can stick to.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Antibodies don't make hormones. They bind to them.
B: Incorrect — The line appears because the antibodies bind to HCG, not because they destroy it.
C: Incorrect — Then every test would show a line, pregnant or not.
D: Correct — No HCG means nothing for the antibodies to bind to, so no line forms.

questions.stem: Which of these is a physical defence that helps a plant stop microorganisms getting in?
options: Poisons in the leaves
Thorns on the stem
Antibacterial chemicals
A tough, waxy cuticle on the leaves
questions.hint: Physical defences are barriers.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is a chemical defence against herbivores.
B: Incorrect — That is a mechanical defence against animals.
C: Incorrect — That is a chemical defence, not a physical one.
D: Correct — The cuticle is a barrier that microorganisms find hard to get through.

questions.stem: How do thorns help a plant?
options: They store water
They deter animals from eating the plant
They kill bacteria
They absorb extra light for photosynthesis
questions.hint: Think about what would happen to an animal that tried to eat it.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Thorns don't store water.
B: Correct — Thorns are a mechanical defence. Hairs do a similar job.
C: Incorrect — Plants use antibacterial chemicals for that.
D: Incorrect — Leaves absorb light. Thorns are for defence.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign that a plant may have a disease?
options: Roots growing downwards
Flowers opening in the sunshine
Leaves growing towards the light
Spots on the leaves
questions.hint: Look for something that has gone wrong with the plant.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is normal, healthy growth.
B: Incorrect — This is normal for many flowering plants.
C: Incorrect — This is normal, healthy growth.
D: Correct — Spots, rot, growths, discolouration and stunted growth can all be signs of disease.

questions.stem: Aphids are small animals that feed on plants. What kind of plant problem are they?
options: Insect pests
A fungus
An ion deficiency
A virus
questions.hint: Think about what kind of living thing an aphid is.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Aphids are insects. Seeing pests on a plant is a sign it may be damaged or diseased.
B: Incorrect — Rose black spot is an example of a fungal disease. Aphids are insects.
C: Incorrect — Ion deficiencies are caused by a lack of minerals, not by animals.
D: Incorrect — Viruses are not animals. TMV is an example of a plant virus.

questions.stem: A plant's leaves have turned yellow because it can't make enough chlorophyll. Which ion is most likely to be missing from the soil?
options: Glucose
Nitrate
Magnesium
Oxygen
questions.hint: This yellowing is called chlorosis.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Glucose is not an ion, and the plant makes it by photosynthesis.
B: Incorrect — A lack of nitrate causes stunted growth, because nitrate is needed for proteins.
C: Correct — Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll, so a lack causes chlorosis.
D: Incorrect — Oxygen is not taken from the soil as an ion.

questions.stem: A farmer wants to find out exactly which pathogen is infecting a crop. Which method could they use?
options: Count the stomata on a leaf
Use a testing kit containing monoclonal antibodies
Water the plant more and see if it recovers
Spray antibiotics and see if the plant recovers
questions.hint: Think about tests that can recognise one particular pathogen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Stomata numbers don't tell you which pathogen is present.
B: Correct — The antibodies bind only to the matching pathogen, so the kit can identify it.
C: Incorrect — This wouldn't identify the pathogen.
D: Incorrect — This wouldn't identify the pathogen, and antibiotics don't work on viruses or fungi.

questions.stem: Some plants make poisons in their leaves. How does this help the plant?
options: It helps the leaves absorb more light
It attracts insects to pollinate the flowers
It deters herbivores from eating it
It stops water being lost from the leaves
questions.hint: Think about which animals eat leaves.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Poisons don't affect how much light is absorbed.
B: Incorrect — Poisons put animals off. They don't attract them.
C: Correct — Poisons are a chemical defence against animals that eat plants.
D: Incorrect — That is the job of the waxy cuticle and the stomata.

questions.stem: Some plants have leaves that droop or curl when they are touched. How might this help the plant?
options: It makes the leaves photosynthesise faster
It kills bacteria on the leaf
It helps the plant take in more carbon dioxide
It can knock off insects or scare away animals that might eat it
questions.hint: Think about an insect or animal landing on the leaf.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Drooping leaves would get less light, not more.
B: Incorrect — Plants use antibacterial chemicals to kill bacteria.
C: Incorrect — Curling leaves doesn't help take in carbon dioxide.
D: Correct — This is a mechanical defence.

questions.stem: How does a cellulose cell wall help a plant resist disease?
options: It makes poisons to deter herbivores
It makes antibodies
It is a tough barrier that makes it harder for microorganisms to get into the cell
It releases chemicals that kill bacteria
questions.hint: Is this a physical, chemical or mechanical defence?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is a chemical defence.
B: Incorrect — Plants don't make antibodies.
C: Correct — Cellulose cell walls are a physical defence.
D: Incorrect — That is a chemical defence. Cellulose works as a barrier.

questions.stem: Why does a plant that is short of nitrate ions show stunted growth?
options: Nitrate is needed to open the stomata
Nitrate is needed to make chlorophyll
Nitrate is needed to make proteins, which are needed for growth
Nitrate is needed to make glucose
questions.hint: Think about which large molecules contain nitrogen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Stomata open when guard cells take in water.
B: Incorrect — That is magnesium. A lack of magnesium causes yellow leaves.
C: Correct — Without enough nitrate the plant can't make enough protein, so it stays small.
D: Incorrect — Glucose is made by photosynthesis from carbon dioxide and water.

questions.stem: The bark on a tree is made of layers of dead cells that fall off. How does this help defend the tree?
options: It is a barrier, and any microorganisms on it fall away with the dead cells
The dead cells release poisons to deter herbivores
The dead cells make antibodies
The dead cells photosynthesise to make extra food
questions.hint: Think about what happens to anything sitting on the outside.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — This is a physical defence that resists invasion by microorganisms.
B: Incorrect — Poisons are a chemical defence. Bark works as a barrier.
C: Incorrect — Plants don't make antibodies.
D: Incorrect — Dead cells can't photosynthesise.

questions.stem: A tomato plant is growing slowly and its leaves have a patchy pattern of light and dark green. A soil test shows normal nitrate and magnesium levels. What is the most likely cause?
options: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)
Rose black spot
Magnesium deficiency
Nitrate deficiency
questions.hint: The soil test rules out two of the options.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — TMV gives a mosaic pattern on the leaves, which reduces photosynthesis and growth.
B: Incorrect — Black spot causes purple or black spots on leaves, not a light and dark green mosaic.
C: Incorrect — The soil test shows magnesium is normal.
D: Incorrect — The soil test shows nitrate is normal.
